Dermatitis.description: Dermatitis is general inflammation of the skin. In dogs it is commonly linked to allergies (food, environmental, flea-bite) or self-trauma from licking, chewing, or scratching, and often appears as red, irritated, or moist patches ('hot spots').
symptoms: Redness, swelling, or moist/oozing patches on the skin
Frequent licking, chewing, or scratching of one area
Hair loss or thinning around the affected patch
Unpleasant odor from the irritated area
Visible discomfort when the area is touched
causes: Skin irritation from moisture trapped in the coat
prevention: Regular grooming and drying the coat after baths/swimming
Consistent flea and parasite control
Identifying and avoiding known allergy triggers where possible
Keeping the dog's living area clean
Prompt attention to minor scratches or irritation before they worsen
recommended_care: Keep the affected area clean and dry
Prevent further licking/scratching (e.g., a protective collar) if advised by a vet
Monitor for spreading or worsening of the patch
Avoid home application of human skin products without veterinary guidance
treatment_information: Veterinarians may recommend topical treatments, medicated shampoos, or anti-inflammatory/antibiotic medication depending on severity and cause
Treatment plans are typically tailored after an in-person examination
when_to_visit_vet: The patch is spreading, bleeding, or has an odor
The dog seems to be in significant discomfort or pain
No improvement within a few days of home hygiene care
Signs of infection (pus, heat, swelling)
Dermatitis.severity: Mild to Moderate (can become serious if infected or left untreated)
Dermatitis.warning: This information is general and educational only. It is not a veterinary diagnosis. A veterinarian should evaluate the dog for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Fungal_infections.description: Fungal skin infections in dogs are caused by fungal organisms (distinct from ringworm, which is a specific dermatophyte fungal infection) affecting the skin, and can cause irritation, hair loss, and changes in skin texture.
symptoms: Patchy hair loss
Flaky, scaly, or crusty skin
Itching or discomfort
Discoloration or thickened skin in affected areas
Unpleasant odor in some cases
causes: Exposure to fungal spores in soil or from other infected animals
Warm, moist environments that favor fungal growth
Weakened immune system or underlying skin conditions
prevention: Keep the dog's skin and coat clean and dry
Avoid prolonged contact with damp bedding or environments
Limit contact with animals known to have fungal infections
Routine grooming to catch early skin changes
recommended_care: Keep affected areas clean and dry
Avoid sharing bedding/grooming tools with other pets during an active infection
Monitor for spread to other parts of the body or to other household pets
treatment_information: Veterinarians may prescribe antifungal shampoos, topical treatments, or oral antifungal medication depending on severity
A confirmed diagnosis (e.g., skin scraping/culture) is typically needed before treatment
when_to_visit_vet: Hair loss or skin changes are spreading
The condition does not improve with basic hygiene care
Other pets or household members develop skin irritation
Signs of secondary bacterial infection appear
Fungal_infections.severity: Moderate (some fungal infections can be contagious to other animals/humans)
Fungal_infections.warning: This information is general and educational only. It is not a veterinary diagnosis. A veterinarian should evaluate the dog for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Healthy.description: The image was classified as showing no visible signs of the skin disease categories in this dataset. This is a general screening result, not a clean bill of health.
symptoms: No visible redness, hair loss, or lesions
Coat appears smooth and evenly distributed
No visible signs of irritation or discomfort
prevention: Maintain a regular grooming routine
Ensure a balanced diet and regular parasite prevention
Schedule routine veterinary check-ups
recommended_care: Continue regular grooming and hygiene practices
Monitor the skin periodically for any new changes
when_to_visit_vet: Any new symptoms (itching, redness, hair loss) appear later
As part of routine annual/bi-annual veterinary wellness checks
Healthy.warning: This is an AI-based screening result, not a veterinary diagnosis or a guarantee of overall health. Continue routine veterinary care.

Hypersensitivity.description: Hypersensitivity reactions occur when a dog's immune system overreacts to a substance (allergen), leading to skin inflammation, itching, and irritation. Common triggers include fleas, food, and environmental allergens.
symptoms: Intense itching or scratching
Redness or inflamed skin, often around the face, ears, paws, or belly
Recurrent skin or ear infections
Swelling in more severe reactions
Restlessness or discomfort
prevention: Consistent flea/parasite prevention
Identifying and avoiding known allergens where possible
Discussing diet trials with a veterinarian if food allergy is suspected
Keeping the living environment clean of common allergens
recommended_care: Keep the skin clean and avoid irritating products
Track flare-ups to help identify potential triggers
treatment_information: Veterinarians may recommend antihistamines, other allergy medications, dietary changes, or allergy testing depending on the case
Severe or recurrent hypersensitivity often benefits from a structured veterinary allergy work-up
when_to_visit_vet: Swelling of the face, lips, or throat (seek immediate veterinary attention)
Difficulty breathing
Frequent or worsening allergic flare-ups
Signs of a secondary skin or ear infection
Hypersensitivity.severity: Moderate (severe allergic/anaphylactic reactions are a medical emergency)
Hypersensitivity.warning: This information is general and educational only. It is not a veterinary diagnosis. Facial swelling or breathing difficulty requires immediate veterinary attention.

demodicosis.description: Demodicosis is caused by an overgrowth of Demodex mites, which naturally live in small numbers on most dogs' skin. When the immune system cannot keep the mite population in check, it can lead to hair loss and skin irritation, particularly in puppies or immunocompromised dogs.
symptoms: Patchy hair loss, often starting around the face, eyes, or forelegs
Red, scaly, or crusty skin
Mild to moderate itching (can vary)
Skin may thicken or darken in chronic cases
Secondary bacterial infection in some cases
causes: Overpopulation of naturally occurring Demodex mites
Immature or weakened immune system (common in young puppies)
Underlying illness or immune suppression in adult dogs
prevention: Maintaining general health and a strong immune system through proper nutrition
Routine veterinary check-ups, especially for puppies
Prompt attention to unexplained hair loss or skin changes
recommended_care: Avoid sharing grooming tools during an active case
Keep the skin clean and monitor for spread
Follow the full course of any prescribed treatment
treatment_information: Veterinarians typically confirm diagnosis via skin scraping and may prescribe miticidal treatments, medicated shampoos, or oral medication
Localized cases in puppies often resolve with the immune system maturing, but should still be monitored by a vet
when_to_visit_vet: Hair loss is spreading or affecting large areas of the body
Signs of skin infection (odor, pus, significant redness)
The dog seems unwell beyond the skin symptoms
No improvement after initial home hygiene care
demodicosis.warning: This information is general and educational only. It is not a veterinary diagnosis. A veterinarian should confirm demodicosis with a skin scraping before treatment.

ringworm.description: Ringworm is not caused by a worm, but by a contagious fungal (dermatophyte) infection of the skin, hair, and nails. It commonly causes circular patches of hair loss and can spread to other pets and humans.
symptoms: Circular or irregular patches of hair loss
Scaly, crusty, or reddened skin at the patch edges
Brittle hair around the affected area
Mild itching in some cases
Lesions may appear on the face, ears, paws, or elsewhere
causes: Contact with an infected animal or contaminated bedding/grooming tools
Higher risk in puppies, senior dogs, or immunocompromised dogs
prevention: Avoid contact with known infected animals
Regularly clean and disinfect bedding, grooming tools, and living areas
Isolate an infected pet from other animals and wash hands after contact
Routine grooming to catch early skin changes
recommended_care: Limit contact between the affected dog and other pets/children during treatment
Disinfect shared surfaces, bedding, and grooming tools
Follow the complete treatment course even if symptoms improve early
treatment_information: Veterinarians may prescribe topical antifungal treatments, medicated shampoos, or oral antifungal medication depending on severity
Diagnosis is typically confirmed via fungal culture or specialized examination
when_to_visit_vet: Circular hair loss patches are spreading
Other pets or household members develop similar skin lesions
No improvement with hygiene measures
The dog is a puppy, senior, or has a known weakened immune system
ringworm.severity: Moderate (highly contagious to other animals and humans - zoonotic)
ringworm.warning: This information is general and educational only. It is not a veterinary diagnosis. Ringworm is contagious to humans; consult a veterinarian and, if needed, a physician for guidance.
